content.title: Block and Inline: Two Different Kinds of Flow
content.hook: Not every element participates in normal flow in exactly the same way.
content.context:
Some elements naturally take a new line in the flow. Other content can stay inside the current line of text.

For this lesson, use a simple model:

- block-like content starts a new row in normal flow;
- inline content can participate inside the current line.
goals: Distinguish block-level and inline behavior well enough to predict why some elements start on a new line while others can share a line.

content.question:
Imagine: ```html

Hello there.

``` Should the strong text normally start a brand-new row?

options.text: Yes. Every element starts a new row.
No. It can participate inside the paragraph's line of text.
Only when the page is wide.
Only when the browser is refreshed.

feedback.correct: The strong element is inline content inside the paragraph. It can stay with the surrounding text.
feedback.incorrect: The strong element is inline content inside the paragraph. It can stay with the surrounding text.

content.title: Compare two paragraphs
content.text:
Now compare: ```html

One paragraph.

Another paragraph.

``` The paragraphs normally occupy separate rows in the document flow. That difference matters. If every element behaved the same way, you would have a much harder time predicting the page.

content.question:
You add another phrase inside the same paragraph: ```html

Read this carefully before continuing.

``` What changes?

options.text: The phrase can remain inside the current line of text.
A new paragraph is automatically created.
The browser moves the phrase to the top of the page.

feedback.correct: The phrase is still part of the paragraph. The inline content can share the paragraph's line.
feedback.incorrect: The phrase is still part of the paragraph. The inline content can share the paragraph's line.

content.prompt:
Create one paragraph containing normal text, a strong word, and another normal phrase. Then create a second paragraph.

Observe which content shares a line and which content starts a new row.
guidelines: State your reasoning clearly in your own words or code.
Compare your response with the reference guide after submitting.
content.sampleResponse: Review your explanation against the core mental model of this lesson.

feedback.correct: Review your explanation against the core mental model of this lesson.
feedback.incorrect: Please write a brief response (at least 10 characters) before submitting.

content.title: Why this matters
content.text:
Layout reasoning starts with the defaults.

If a piece of content appears on a different line than you expected, the first useful question is not “Which fancy layout tool fixes this?”

It is:

**“What does this element normally do in flow?”**

content.question: A heading is followed by a paragraph, and a bold phrase appears inside that paragraph. Which pattern is the expected normal-flow behavior?

options.text: Heading, then paragraph on the next row; the bold phrase stays within the paragraph's line.
Every word becomes its own row.

feedback.correct: The heading and paragraph establish separate blocks in normal flow. The bold phrase remains part of the paragraph's inline content.
feedback.incorrect: The heading and paragraph establish separate blocks in normal flow. The bold phrase remains part of the paragraph's inline content.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** Normal flow has different element behaviors. Learn those defaults before trying to override them.
**Senior habit:** When layout surprises you, first ask what the element normally does.
**Mastery signal:** You can predict whether simple HTML will continue the current line or start a new row.
